title: Peripheral Arterial Claudication
subject: Medicine
summary: Pain on exertion due to arterial narrowing, relieved by rest. Diagnosis hinges on history, pulse exam, and ankle‑brachial index. Management is lifestyle change, antiplatelets, and revascularisation when needed.

sections.p: Peripheral arterial claudication is pain or cramping in the lower limbs that starts with exertion, is reproducible, and resolves within minutes of rest. It reflects inadequate blood flow through narrowed arteries.
b: Exertional pain, fixed distance, rapid relief, reproducible

t.b: Compares ankle systolic pressure to arm pressure; an ABI <0.90 indicates PAD.
Useful when ABI is falsely normal due to medial arterial calcification.
Shows monophasic pattern in severe stenosis; absent or biphasic suggests critical disease.

sections.p: The Fontaine classification stages claudication from I (intermittent claudication) to IV (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene). The Rutherford categories further refine severity and guide treatment urgency.

t.b: Quantifies functional impairment; higher scores need more aggressive therapy.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, atherosclerosis remains the main driver, but infections, rheumatic disease, and sickle cell can also precipitate claudication.
b: Rheumatic heart disease (valvular lesions causing low flow)

t.b: Detects HIV; positive status raises risk of vasculitis and accelerated atherosclerosis.
Rules out cardiac causes of exertional pain.

sections.p: Patients describe a burning or cramping pain in calves, thighs, or buttocks that starts after a set distance and stops with rest. Pain may be bilateral and can be accompanied by numbness or coldness.
b: Rapid relief after 1–2 minutes of rest

t.b: Absent or diminished dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pulses indicate arterial narrowing.
Look for pallor, hair loss, or ulceration.

sections.p: Investigations confirm PAD, assess severity, and rule out mimics. In resource‑limited settings, ABI and pulse exam are first steps; Doppler and imaging are added if available.

From infected ulcers; look for fever, tachycardia, and elevated WBC.

sections.p: Treatment focuses on risk factor modification, antiplatelet therapy, and revascularisation for symptomatic or high‑risk patients.
b: Lifestyle changes: smoking cessation, exercise, diet

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, ABI, and risk factors is essential. Preventive measures include tight glycaemic control, blood pressure management, and vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus.

whenToSeekHelp: Rest pain, ulceration, gangrene, sudden worsening of claudication

faq.q: What is the most reliable bedside test for PAD?
faq.a: Ankle‑brachial index; an ABI <0.90 confirms disease.

faq.q: Why is aspirin preferred over clopidogrel in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Aspirin is cheaper, widely available, and has a well‑established safety profile.

faq.q: Can claudication be caused by a venous problem?
faq.a: No; venous disease causes swelling and pain that improves with elevation, not exertion.

exam: What history question helps differentiate claudication from cardiac angina? — Ask if pain is reproducible with a fixed walking distance and relieved by rest within minutes.
Which investigation is first-line when a patient has suspected PAD but no imaging available? — ABI measurement.
Why is a monophasic Doppler waveform significant? — Indicates severe arterial narrowing or occlusion.
In a patient with diabetes and claudication, what drug class should be avoided and why? — NSAIDs; they worsen renal function and can mask pain.
What is the next step if a patient with Fontaine II claudication has an ABI of 0.75? — Consider revascularisation if symptoms persist despite optimal medical therapy.
When is urgent revascularisation indicated in PAD? — Presence of rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene (critical limb ischemia).
